title: NRI University Team Beats 65,000 to Win Global Quantum Challenge
excerpt: Three data-science students from Dr. RVR NRI Institute of Technology in Andhra Pradesh took the top prize at the WISER Vanguard Global Challenge with THRINETRA, a project applying quantum technology to workforce management.
body:
• Three data-science students from Dr. RVR NRI Institute of Technology (Deemed to be University) in Andhra Pradesh have won the WISER Vanguard Global Challenge, an international quantum-technology innovation competition.
  • Their winning project, THRINETRA – Quantum Workforce Optimisation, explores how quantum technology can be used to optimise workforce management.
  • The competition drew around 65,000 participants from 33 countries; 219 teams were shortlisted, and the NRI University team made the final top 10 before taking the overall prize.
  • NRI families weighing Indian universities should note the pipeline behind this win: a WISER-run quantum training programme in Andhra Pradesh, backed by the state government, has registered 50,000-plus students, with top performers offered exposure visits, lab internships and industry placements.

Three students from Dr. RVR NRI Institute of Technology (Deemed to be University) in Andhra Pradesh have beaten around 65,000 competitors from 33 countries to win the WISER Vanguard Global Challenge, an international competition focused on innovation in quantum technology. The team — G. Tejaswi Venkata Aparna, Shaik Muntaz and R. Madhusudhana Rao, all from the university’s Data Science Department — took the top prize with THRINETRA – Quantum Workforce Optimisation, a project exploring how quantum technology can be used to optimise workforce management.

A pipeline victory, not a fluke

The win was announced by the institution on September 25, according to The Hindu, which reported that 219 teams had been shortlisted for the global challenge. It did not come out of nowhere. As part of the Amaravati Quantum Valley Initiative, 200 NRI University students received training in quantum technology. One university team made the final top 10; that team then took the overall prize.

https://x.com/OwenGregorian/status/2108542444836880665

The Washington Institute for STEM, Entrepreneurship and Research (WISER), the Washington DC-based organisation running the programme, says it is working with the Andhra Pradesh government to train 50,000 students across the state. In December 2025 it announced registrations had crossed 50,000, calling it the world’s largest quantum training programme. The initiative sits at the core of Andhra Pradesh’s new Quantum Policy and the plan to build Amaravati into a quantum hub — branded Quantum Valley — aligned with India’s National Quantum Mission.

Why the win matters

Quantum technology is widely treated as the next strategic frontier in computing, communications and cybersecurity, and the race to train a quantum-ready workforce is as intense as the race to build the machines themselves. The THRINETRA project is a case study in that race: applying quantum thinking to workforce optimisation — the scheduling and deployment of people — is exactly the kind of applied, real-world problem the field needs to solve if quantum computing is to move beyond the laboratory.

The win also validates a bet the Andhra Pradesh government has made at scale. Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has publicly backed the WISER programme as a “quantum leap” in technology adoption, aimed at turning the state into a globally competitive deep-tech centre. A global title from a cohort of 200 trained students is the kind of early proof point such a policy needs.

What it means for the diaspora

For NRIs, there are two connections. The first is institutional: WISER itself is a Washington DC-based body, and the programme linking it to Andhra Pradesh is a genuine India–US bridge in a technology both countries treat as strategic. WISER also runs the US Commerce Department-funded Elevate Quantum tech hub and has run quantum hackathons with NYU Abu Dhabi and the Open Quantum Institute at CERN, placing the NRI students’ win inside a genuinely global ecosystem. The second is personal: families abroad who have seen Indian campuses primarily as feeders of talent to foreign universities are now watching a homegrown institution take a world title in one of the hardest fields in technology.

What’s next

NRI University Chancellor R. Venkat Rao and Vice-Chancellor K.R.S. Sambasiva Rao congratulated the students on the achievement. WISER says its Andhra Pradesh programme will expand in 2026 into deeper technical modules, hands-on experimentation and industry-aligned research pathways, with high performers getting exposure visits, internships in national and international quantum laboratories, and support into specialised placements. For the three winners, the immediate prize is the title itself — and a place on the map in a field where, until recently, Indian campuses were barely on the starting grid.
